name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Components and working of an electrostatic precipitator

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram below represents an electrostatic precipitator used in thermal power plants to remove particulate matter from exhaust gases. Identify the parts labelled X and Y along with their correct functions.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic shows dirty air entering a chamber from the left, passing first across a vertical array of circular cross-section wires surrounded by a halo (labelled X), then flowing between horizontal parallel plates (labelled Y) before exiting as clean air on the right.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Air flows from left to right at a velocity low enough between the parallel plates to allow separated dust particles to settle and fall.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
An electrostatic precipitator removes over \(99\%\) of particulate matter from thermal power plant exhaust using electrostatic attraction between negatively charged dust particles and grounded collecting plates.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Component X represents the electrode wires maintained at several thousand volts, which produce a discharge corona that releases electrons.
2. These electrons attach to dust particles in the dirty air, giving them a net negative charge.
3. Component Y represents the grounded collection plates, which attract the negatively charged dust particles as the air passes between them, leaving clean air to exit.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Unlike a scrubber (which uses a spray of water or lime to remove gases like \(\text{SO}_2\)), an electrostatic precipitator uses high-voltage negatively charged wires (X) and grounded collection plates (Y). Therefore, X is negatively charged electrode wires producing a corona that releases electrons, and Y is grounded collection plates that attract charged dust particles.

answer.text: X: Water/lime spray nozzle that absorbs \(\text{SO}_2\); Y: Grounded collection plates
X: Negatively charged electrode wires producing a corona that releases electrons; Y: Grounded collection plates that attract negatively charged dust particles
X: Grounded electrode wires that neutralise dust; Y: Negatively charged collection plates that repel dust particles
X: Platinum-palladium catalyst mesh; Y: High-voltage plates that oxidise unburnt hydrocarbons

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Effect of sewage discharge on dissolved oxygen and BOD in a river

questiontext.text: The graph below shows changes in two water quality parameters, P and Q, along the direction of flow of a river after domestic sewage is discharged at the indicated point. Identify P and Q, and determine where fish kill and disappearance of clean-water organisms occur.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots concentration on the vertical axis against direction of river flow on the horizontal axis, with a sewage discharge point near the left. Curve P is initially low, rises sharply at the sewage discharge point, and decreases downstream. Curve Q is initially high, drops sharply to near zero at the sewage discharge point, and recovers downstream.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Upstream of the sewage discharge point represents clean river water with low organic load and high dissolved oxygen. Downstream progression represents natural biodegradation and reaeration along the river flow.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) measures the amount of biodegradable organic matter in sewage water. Micro-organisms decomposing this organic matter consume dissolved oxygen (DO) from the water body.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Domestic sewage adds large amounts of biodegradable organic matter, causing BOD (curve P) to spike immediately at the point of discharge.
2. Micro-organisms multiplying on this organic matter consume dissolved oxygen rapidly, causing a sharp decline in DO (curve Q) immediately downstream.
3. Because aquatic organisms require dissolved oxygen for respiration, the sharp drop in DO immediately downstream leads to fish kill and the disappearance of clean-water organisms.
4. Further downstream, as organic matter is consumed, BOD (P) declines and DO (Q) recovers, allowing clean-water organisms to reappear.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Curve P represents Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), curve Q represents Dissolved Oxygen (DO), and fish kill occurs immediately downstream of the sewage discharge point where Q drops sharply.

answer.text: P is Dissolved Oxygen (DO), Q is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD); fish kill occurs far downstream where P rises.
P is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), Q is Dissolved Oxygen (DO); fish kill occurs upstream before sewage discharge.
P is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), Q is Dissolved Oxygen (DO); fish kill occurs immediately downstream of sewage discharge where Q drops sharply.
P is Nitrate concentration, Q is Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD); fish kill occurs where P is minimum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Biomagnification of DDT across aquatic trophic levels

questiontext.text: The diagram below depicts the biomagnification of DDT in an aquatic food chain. Identify the DDT concentrations at levels X and Y, and state the major physiological consequence observed in fish-eating birds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The trophic flow diagram shows DDT concentrations increasing from Water (\(0.003\text{ ppb}\)) to Zooplankton (\(0.04\text{ ppm}\)), then to Small fish (X), Large fish (\(2\text{ ppm}\)), and finally Fish-eating birds (Y).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Upward arrows indicate trophic transfer of persistent toxicant DDT from prey to predator in an aquatic food chain. Note the unit change from parts per billion (\(\text{ppb}\)) in water to parts per million (\(\text{ppm}\)) in organisms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a non-biodegradable, non-excretable toxicant at successive trophic levels. High DDT concentrations in birds interfere with calcium metabolism.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In the aquatic food chain, DDT concentration rises from \(0.003\text{ ppb}\) in water to \(0.04\text{ ppm}\) in zooplankton.
2. At the small fish level (X), DDT concentration increases further to \(0.5\text{ ppm}\), which lies between \(0.04\text{ ppm}\) (zooplankton) and \(2\text{ ppm}\) (large fish).
3. At the top trophic level of fish-eating birds (Y), DDT concentration reaches \(25\text{ ppm}\).
4. High concentrations of DDT disturb calcium metabolism in birds, causing thinning of eggshells and their premature breaking, eventually leading to a decline in bird populations.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking monotonicity: \(0.003\text{ ppb} \lt 0.04\text{ ppm} \lt 0.5\text{ ppm} \lt 2\text{ ppm} \lt 25\text{ ppm}\). Thus, X \(= 0.5\text{ ppm}\), Y \(= 25\text{ ppm}\), and high DDT disturbs calcium metabolism in birds, causing thinning of eggshells.

answer.text: X \(= 0.5\text{ ppm}\), Y \(= 25\text{ ppm}\); high DDT disturbs calcium metabolism, causing thinning of eggshells.
X \(= 0.05\text{ ppm}\), Y \(= 250\text{ ppm}\); high DDT causes cultural eutrophication in bird habitats.
X \(= 0.5\text{ ppb}\), Y \(= 25\text{ ppb}\); high DDT causes snow-blindness and cataracts in birds.
X \(= 1.5\text{ ppm}\), Y \(= 10\text{ ppm}\); high DDT enhances calcification of eggshells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ENVIRONMENTALISSUES_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Relative contribution of greenhouse gases to global warming

questiontext.text: The pie chart below shows the relative contribution of four major greenhouse gases (W, X, Y, and Z) to total global warming. Identify W, X, Y, and Z.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The pie chart divides total global warming contributions among four greenhouse gases: W contributes \(60\%\), X contributes \(20\%\), Y contributes \(14\%\), and Z contributes \(6\%\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The four sectors together account for \(100\%\) of the relative contributions of major greenhouse gases to total global warming.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Greenhouse gases absorb long-wave infrared radiation re-emitted by Earth's surface and radiate heat energy back toward Earth, driving global warming.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. The largest contributor at \(60\%\) (W) is carbon dioxide (\(\text{CO}_2\)).
2. The second largest contributor at \(20\%\) (X) is methane (\(\text{CH}_4\)).
3. The third contributor at \(14\%\) (Y) is chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
4. The smallest of the four contributors at \(6\%\) (Z) is nitrous oxide (\(\text{N}_2\text{O}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Summing the percentages: \(60\% + 20\% + 14\% + 6\% = 100\%\). Therefore, W is Carbon dioxide, X is Methane, Y is CFCs, and Z is Nitrous oxide (\(\text{N}_2\text{O}\)).
